raw_case_text: More recently, we experienced the second case of disseminated-CL in Ecuador, which was clinically very similar to diffuse-CL. The patient was a 43-year-old male, as of February 22, 2006 (Fig. 2c, d), and came from a small community "Barrio 28 de Enero," Chimborazo province, a subtropical mountainous area at the beginning of Andean slopes, located at 500 m a.s.l. (Fig. 1 (3)). The lesion began with an insect bite-like papular lesion on the forearm. Then, the lesions appeared on the right ear and the nose. About 2 years later, lesions appeared on a wide range of the lower extremities, followed by multiple and confluent lesions on the abdomen, thorax, body side, and thigh (photographs not shown). A superficial involvement of mucosae of the nose and upper lip was observed as seen in Fig. 4a. At the time of examination in the National Institute of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, the patient already received injections of nine ampoules of trivalent antimonials Repodral  (20 mg/kg/day) at a rural health center (Cumanda, Guayas province). After finishing several courses of the treatment, the patient received Glucantime  (10 mg/kg/day) during about 5 months and responded well to the treatment. Montenegro skin test showed positive with a 17-mm induration, and rK39 kit test revealed a strongly positive band, suggesting a higher level of functions of the humoral immune system(s). Smear specimens, skin biopsies, syringe aspirates for in vitro cultures, and materials on FTA  classic cards (Whatman ) were taken from the active lesions. The smear specimen revealed positive for the Leishmania amastigote with a scanty number. Promastigotes grown in vitro had a tendency to decrease gradually after several days of cultivation and then totally disappeared, probably because of the effect of previous treatment with Repodral  before the material aspiration for culture. The parasites from the biopsy and FTA  card materials were identified as L. (V.) guyanensis by PCR analysis (Fig. 3). Thus, the case was clinically very similar to diffuse-CL but showed the following marked differences: (1) the organisms isolated were identified as the subgenus Viannia, L. (V.) guyanensis, which is also known as one of the causative agents of disseminated-CL in different endemic countries of the New World; (2) the patient was sensitive against antimonials; and (3) the superficial involvement of mucosae was recognized as seen in Fig. 2c, such a mucosal sign is never seen in diffuse-CL cases. The patient was alcoholic, and complications of his liver cirrhosis led to the unexpected death after healing of disseminated-CL.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old male presented with chronic widespread papulonodular skin lesions and superficial mucosal involvement of the nose and upper lip.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 43-year-old male presented in February 2006 with widespread cutaneous eruptions. The illness began as an insect bite-like papule on the forearm, followed by papules on the right ear and nose. Over 2 years, lesions spread widely across the lower extremities, followed by multiple confluent plaques on the abdomen, thorax, flanks, and thighs, with superficial involvement of the mucosa of the nose and upper lip. He received 9 ampoules of trivalent antimonial (Repodral, 20 mg/kg/day) at a rural health center prior to presentation at the National Institute of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of chronic severe alcoholism and liver cirrhosis. Resident of Barrio 28 de Enero, Chimborazo province, Ecuador (subtropical mountainous area at 500 m a.s.l.). Pretreated with 9 ampoules of trivalent antimonial (Repodral).
subjective.review_of_systems: Widespread skin eruptions, nasal and lip mucosal irritation; denied sensory loss, motor weakness, or focal neurological symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Extensive, confluent papular and nodular lesions distributed across the right ear, nose, thorax, abdomen, flanks, thighs, and lower extremities. Superficial mucosal infiltration and erosions involving the nasal mucosa and upper lip. Neurological examination showed completely intact cutaneous sensation without peripheral nerve enlargement.
objective.routine_investigations: Stigmata and laboratory markers of chronic liver cirrhosis documented in context.
objective.advanced_workup: Smear specimens, skin punch biopsies, syringe aspirates, and FTA classic card samples obtained. Giemsa-stained smears showed intracellular microorganisms in scanty numbers. In vitro culture yielded promastigotes that gradually declined and cleared, attributed to prior antimonial therapy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis (disseminated-CL) with mucosal involvement caused by Leishmania (Viannia) guyanensis in a patient with alcoholic liver cirrhosis.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Direct smear specimens positive for Leishmania amastigotes. PCR analysis of skin biopsy and FTA card specimens identified Leishmania (Viannia) guyanensis. Montenegro skin test was positive with 17 mm induration; rK39 rapid kit test showed a strongly positive band.
Differentials Ruled Out: Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL; ruled out by positive Montenegro skin test, subgenus Viannia etiology, mucosal involvement, and response to antimonials) and lepromatous leprosy.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Following initial therapy with Repodral (20 mg/kg/day, 9 ampoules), patient received meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime) at 10 mg/kg/day for approximately 5 months, achieving complete clinical healing of cutaneous and mucosal lesions. Patient subsequently died due to decompensated liver cirrhosis related to chronic alcoholism.
